newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani Islamist launches anti-Bhutto campaign.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani Islamist launches anti-Bhutto campaign.

text.p: The leader of a Pakistani fundamentalist Islamist party launched a new campaign against Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto on Tuesday, vowing to hold daily demonstrations to demand her removal.
"We will start demonstrations across the country from today," Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) chief Qazi Hussain Ahmed told a rally of several thousand people in Rawalpindi, near the capital Islamabad.
"The President (Farooq Leghari) should immediately remove Bhutto and dissolve the (national and provincial) assemblies," he said amid chants from the crowd demanding Bhutto's removal.
Ahmed accuses Bhutto of corruption, incompetence and promoting Western and Indian culture in Pakistan. The prime minister denies the charges.
Ahmed was speaking a day after his party's plans to stage a million-strong protest sit-in before the parliament building in Islamabad fizzled out.

On Monday, the police arrested and later released Ahmed, as well as his deputies Khurshid Ahmed and Ghafoor Ahmed, on the second day of chaotic skirmishes with militants in Islamabad and Rawalpindi. At least 50 people were injured in the clashes.
Security measures were relaxed on Tuesday, though security forces blocked access roads to Islamabad to prevent protesters from reaching parliament.
Paramilitary troops were brought into the capital to guard parliament, the prime minister's secretariat, the president's house, the foreign ministry and the diplomatic enclave.
Most schools and universities in Islamabad remained closed for the third day and many people did not go to work.

A trial of strength between Pakistan's Islamic militants and Bhutto's security forces had crippled normal life in Islamabad for the three days, owing mainly to the Islamic party's strong base in student politics.
The JI has long shown more skill at mobilising its youthful adherents for battles with police than for winning votes in Pakistan's fragile democracy.

It has a long history of bitter rivalry with Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) and won just three seats in the 217-seat National Assembly (lower house) at the last general election in October 1993, which brought Bhutto to power.
All three JI members of parliament resigned their seats on Saturday, following the example of Ahmed, who quit his Senate (upper house) seat last month as part of his anti-Bhutto drive.
While they have never enjoyed much success at the polls, the JI and other Islamist parties exert a political influence disproportionate to their popularity.
